To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

suboptimal posterior inference in variational inference is often due, not to the limited complexity of variational distributions, but to amortizing inference, and that the parameters used in the recognition model to increase the complexity of the variational approximation are also used to improve generalization.

the suboptimal inference in variational inference can be attributed to the amortization and the generator learning to adapt to the choice of the approximation, which is not the same as increasing the expressiveness of approximating distributions.

the quality of approximate inference in variatational autoencoders can be improved by a) using more complex variational distributions and b) using the parameters of the variational distributions to learn a more flexible inference procedure.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions:
How do we measure suboptimality of inference in VAEs?
How does the generator influence the quality of inference?
How does the capacity of the inference network generalize over all datapoints?

the following: (1) understanding the role of the variational approximation in inference, (2) the role of the recognition network in generalizing inference over all datapoint and (3) the interaction between the generator and the inference model in amortized inference.
understanding the factors that contribute to the quality of inference in amortized inference algorithms and how these factors affect the generalization of the inference procedure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
suboptimal approximate inference in VAEs is not due to the limited complexity of approximating distribution.

the quality of approximate inference in VAE is not solely determined by the complexity of the variational family but also by the ability of the generator to adapt to the choice of approximation and by the capacity of the encoder to generalize over the dataset.
the suboptimal posterior inference is not due to the limited complexity of variational distributions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show the importance of the capacity of the inference network to learn a general inference procedure, and the importance of the parameters used to improve the expressiveness of inference.
we show that the quality of inference in variational approximations can often be improved by simply increasing the capacity of the inference network.
the capacity of the inference model is a more significant factor in determining the quality of posterior approximation in amortized inference than the complexity of the approximant.
The main takeaway from our work is that
inference suboptimality in amortized inference is a consequence of the optimization objective, and that the choice of variational distribution is not the main culprit.
inference suboptimality in variational inference is often due the amortization of inference rather than the expressiveness of approximation.
the choice of approximation should be made with the aim of generalizing inference over all datapoint, rather than just improving the approximation complexity.
